name: Nico Collins
body_compact: A 24.6% target share, WR18, paired with a WR8 finish among qualifying receivers at 1,117 yards: that is who Collins was last year, and our number has him at 253 points, WR11, a full 32 points over what WRs drafted around pick 16 have historically delivered. The catch is scoring. His red-zone share of touches was just WR64, and his points per game slid from 17.55 to 14.95. That dip is why he is here and not ten picks higher. He is going a round later than he should. Take him.
body_full:
The case starts with the target share. A 24.6% cut of Houston's throws is WR18 territory, and our projection leans on it staying there: 25% targets is worth 10.1 points a game to us, net of the factors around it. Add a 33.4% air-yards share and a 76.9% snap share, and he's getting first-receiver volume in an offense the books posted a 9.5 win total on. Our number lands at 253 points, WR11 on our board.

Drafters have him around pick 16, a round earlier than last September and still too patient. WRs taken at that spot have historically scored about 220 with busts and injuries pooled in. We have him 32.7 points clear of that. There are four receivers left in his tier before a 16.8-point cliff, so waiting for someone behind him is betting against the gap.

The real knock is last season's dip: 17.55 points a game in 2024 fell to 14.95 in 2025, and his red-zone share of his own touches was only 15.6%, WR64. Nineteen red-zone touches and 10 inside the ten say the team still funneled him scoring chances, so the dip reads more like a down year than a broken role. He cleared 15 points in 7 of 15 weeks and beat the position's median in 14 of them.

Games are the other guardrail: he's played 12, 15 and 15 the last three years, so 12 is in his history. I'd take him a round earlier than his ADP and not lose sleep over the dip.

name: Brock Bowers
body_compact: He went TE1 two years ago, missed four games last season and still finished TE11 while topping the position's weekly median in 11 of 12 starts. The target load never wavered, 23.6%, second only to Trey McBride. Week 9 alone was 43.3 points, a spike week the red-zone role supposedly rules out, and the new staff kept him listed first among the LV tight ends. The worry is the red-zone work, just 19.3% of his touches, which caps the spike weeks. Still, we have him at 214 points, 20 better than TEs drafted around pick 20. Take him there.
body_full:
Two years ago he was the TE1 in fantasy with 262.7 points across a full 17. Last year injuries took four games and he still ended TE11, beating the position's weekly median in 11 of his 12 starts at 14.5 points a game. The usage explains why: a 23.6% target share, second at the position behind only Trey McBride. He was on the field for 85.5% of the snaps, TE7 among qualifying tight ends, and his 66 touches ranked TE9. That workload is the case, and it survived a 3-win team and a coaching staff that is now entirely new under Klint Kubiak. He's 23.7 on opening day, entering his third season after going in the first round at pick 13.

The catch shows up inside the ten. Only 19.3% of his touches came in the red zone, TE45 among qualifying tight ends, and his 6.5-yard average depth of target ranks 41st. He gets fed short and often, which is steady but limits the monster weeks, that 43.3-point week 9 being the exception rather than a pattern. If the new staff pushes him closer to the goal line, the ceiling opens up. If not, he's a high-volume points machine.

Games are the real question. We expect 15 starts, with 10 to 17 the realistic spread, and his 2025 season effectively ended after week 16. Our number has him at 214 points, about 20 better than what TEs drafted around pick 20 have historically given. One player sits in his tier before a 48.4-point drop behind him. Drafters take him around pick 20 and that's fair. I'd grab him there without hesitating, because the replacement gap is real.

name: Trey McBride
body_compact: The red-zone touches say TE1, 33 of them last season, but only 19.5% of his own touches came inside the 20, TE44 among 126. The touchdowns were volume-driven, and now Mike LaFleur and Nathaniel Hackett are new to the play sheet. Still, 316 points, TE1 among 126, above the weekly median all 17 weeks, and our number has him 20 points clear of TEs drafted around pick 21. The team around him won 3 games and the books opened week one at an 18-point total, so the passing volume has to hold. He is our TE1 at overall rank 49. Draft him, no hesitation.
body_full:
He cleared the weekly median in all 17 games last season and finished TE1 among 126 qualifying tight ends at 18.6 points a game, up from 15.2 the year before. That is a full leap in role, not a spike. Our number puts him at 215 points, about 20 over the historical return for TEs drafted around pick 21, and he is our TE1 at overall rank 49. The middle range runs 185 to 245, so most outcomes still make him worth a late second.

The wrinkle is how the points got there. He led all tight ends with 33 red-zone touches and 1,239 yards, but only 19.5% of his own touches came inside the 20, TE44 among 126. His average target sat 6.7 yards downfield, TE38. The scoring leaned on getting there often, and Arizona got there rarely in a 3-win season. If the new staff, Mike LaFleur as head coach and Nathaniel Hackett calling plays, runs fewer plays or stalls closer to midfield, the 18.6 a game has real room to slip.

Availability is the quiet strength. He played 17, 16 and 17 the last three years, and the sheet expects 15 with a range of 12 to 17. That reliability at tight end is worth a round on its own. The books posted 57.5 receiving yards and 6.5 catches on him this season, which reads like they expect the role to carry over. He is first on the depth chart, no injury designation on file, and the tier behind him drops off hard, 48.4 points before the next name. Draft him at his ADP. Waiting on him would cost you, because he is a steal at pick 21.

name: Jonathan Taylor
body_compact: Our number has him at 236 points, RB6, and drafters are taking him around pick 12, a round later than he should go. Last season he scored 360 at RB4, cleared 15 points in 10 of 17 weeks, and played every game. The worry is the touchdown load: a 33.3% touchdown-points share costs him 6.2 a game when it cools, and 2023 was a 10-game year. Still, 74 red-zone touches and 40 inside the ten make the scoring repeatable. Draft him at 12, and if he slides toward 15, that is a steal.
body_full:
The case starts with the scoring. Last season he ran for 74 red-zone touches and 40 inside the ten, both RB2, one spot behind Christian McCaffrey, and he scored above the weekly median in 16 of 17 games. His points per game climbed from 17.48 in 2024 to 21.19 last year, and his target share rose with it, from 8.0% to 10.4%. That is why our number sits at 236 and why he is RB6 on our board while drafters take him around pick 12, a round later than he should go.

The downside is real and it has a number. A 33.3% touchdown-points share costs him 6.2 a game when the touchdowns cool, and the red-zone and inside-ten shares each shave another 1.4 to 1.6. That is what a heavy scoring profile looks like on paper. The counter is volume: 369 touches, RB2, on an 82.4% snap share, with the same coaching staff back. He cleared 15 points in 10 of his 17 weeks, so the scoring did not ride on one spike even with that 49.6-point week 10. The 2023 season is the other shadow, a 10-game year, and our expected 15 games ranges down to 9 if injury hits.

The books posted him at 76.5 rush yards and 2.5 receptions a game, which reads like they expect the rushing role to hold. His ADP has drifted down, from 7.4 to 7.7, so nobody is rushing on him either. Six players sit in his tier before a 17.1-point drop, so waiting past pick 12 means picking from the next group. Take him at 12. If he slides a few picks after that, it is a steal.

name: Chase Brown
body_compact: The red-zone work is the soft spot: 47 red-zone touches look fine until you see just 14.7% of his own touches came there, RB74 among 146 backs. But the receiving profile carries him, 414 yards and a target share that jumped from 11.2% to 14.5%, all in an offense Zac Taylor still calls himself. He played all 17 games last year and went over the weekly median 16 times. Our board has him RB5, drafters are waiting until pick 18, and seven guys sit in his tier before a 17.1-point drop. I'd take him a round earlier than his ADP.
body_full:
Our board has Chase Brown as RB5 and 32nd overall, but drafters keep letting him slide to around pick 18. That gap is the whole case. Our number puts him at 236 points, about 20 clear of what backs drafted in that spot have historically returned even with the busts pooled in, and there are still seven players in his tier before the group drops off by 17.1 points. A tier that deep at a position this thin is worth reaching for a round early.

The shape of last season was reliability with a receiving floor... not that word, let me say it plainly: he cleared the position's weekly median in 16 of 17 games and never dipped below 6 points in a week. The target share climbed from 11.2% to 14.5%, and the books posted him at 3.5 receptions and 22.5 receiving yards a game this year, so they expect that role to hold. He touched the ball 301 times, top ten among qualifying backs, and Zac Taylor is still the one calling plays.

The real wart is scoring-range usage. Only 14.7% of his touches came inside the red zone, RB74 among 146, even though he finished RB13 in red-zone touches and touches inside the ten. The volume is there, the share of it that converts to touchdowns is thin, and that caps the ceiling on weeks you need a spike. He played all 17 games in 2025 and 16 the year before, so the availability range of 10 to 17 feels cautious. Draft him ahead of his ADP and don't overthink it.

name: Drake London
body_compact: Drake London went WR4 in 2024, then injuries cut him to 12 games last year and WR22. He still commanded a 30% target share, fifth among receivers, and the Falcons handed the offense to Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees with London first on the depth chart. Our number puts him at 268 points, 28 ahead of what receivers drafted around pick 13 usually give you. The catch: he scored above the weekly median in 11 of 12 games yet finished WR22, so the week-to-week was there and the ceiling plays were not. Take him at 13 if you want the target hog. A round earlier is a reach.
body_full:
The 2025 season is the whole argument. Twelve games, 200 points, WR22, after a 280-point, WR4 year in 2024. Four weeks lost to injury from weeks 12 to 15, and a healthy week he did not play. But he cleared 15 points in half his weeks and beat the position's median in 11 of 12, so the per-week production never dipped. The total collapsed because he missed a month, not because the role did.

And the role is untouched. He's listed first among Atlanta's receivers with Dotson, Zaccheaus and Branch behind him, he played 90% of snaps, and he ate 30% of the targets and 30% of the air yards. Our number has him at 268 points, WR9 overall, about 28 points better than what receivers drafted around pick 13 have historically given back, busts and injuries pooled in.

Two things hold him back from the top five. His red-zone share of touches was just 13.4%, WR86, and his average depth of target was 10.9 yards, WR122, so last year's scoring leaned on week 9's 38.8 more than steady touchdowns. But he took 8 touches inside the ten, WR9 among 225, so the chances near the goal line were there. The books posted his receiving line at 64.5 yards and 5.5 catches, and their win total for Atlanta sits at 7.5. Stefanski and Rees are both new, and nobody knows yet what that offense looks like. He's one of six players left in his tier before a 16.8-point cliff, so if you miss the run, the drop is real. At pick 13 I'd draft him. A round earlier, I'd want to see the new offense first.

name: George Pickens
body_compact: Pickens just turned a 17-game season into 290 points and WR5, and the usage came back with him: 22.6% of Dallas targets, 31.4% of the air yards. The downside is real, he was WR51 in red-zone share of his own touches, and Lamb still sits first on the depth chart. Our number puts him at 271, ahead of the 238 history says for WRs at this spot, and there are seven players left before a 16.8-point cliff. Drafters moved him up five picks since early September and they are right. Take him at pick 21 and sleep fine.
body_full:
The season that decides this is the one he just played: 17 games, 290 points, WR5, 1429 yards that trailed only Puka Nacua among qualifying receivers, and he beat the weekly position median in 16 of 17 weeks. That is not a spike built on one fluky month. He went from 11.74 points a game in 2024 to 17.05 last year, so the leap held up across a full season, and he is 25.5 entering year five.

The usage is why I believe it holds. 22.6% of the targets is worth 9.2 points a game on its own, the 81.6% snap share adds another 6.2, and 31.4% of the team's air yards means the deep part of the field runs through him. Lamb is listed first and the target room is crowded enough to cost him about a point a game, but Pickens got 23 red-zone touches last year, WR3 among qualifiers, so the scoring chances are already arriving.

Our number has him at 271, a WR8 we think beats the roughly 238 that WRs drafted around pick 21 have historically put up, busts and injuries pooled in. Availability is the one thing to respect: 15 games expected, with 11 as the low end. He has missed time once in three seasons, two weeks in 2024, so the 17-game year is more the rule than the exception. Take him at 21. Seven players sit in his tier before a 16.8-point drop, and waiting past that stretch costs you real points.

name: Chris Olave
body_compact: Nine receivers share his tier before a 16.8-point drop behind him, and we have him at 274 points, WR6 overall. Drafters take him around pick 18, which is a round later than a WR6 should go. The case is usage: 29% target share and half the team's air yards, both worth real points a game. The real downside is availability. He played 8 of 17 in 2024 with a concussion ending his year, and 16 of 17 in 2025 before an illness ended that one. Our 15-game expectation already shades that. Draft him at 18. If he slips past the teens, that's a steal.
body_full:
The number that should drive your pick here is the tier. We have nine players left in his tier before a 16.8-point cliff, and we put Olave at 274 points, WR6 on our board. Drafters take him around pick 18, and WR6 going at 18 is a round later than he should. Our number is +28.3 over the history of receivers drafted where he's going, and that history already pools in the busts and injuries. He doesn't need to beat his own 2025 to win you the pick.

The usage is what makes me trust it. 29% target share, 84% of the snaps, and half the team's air yards at 49.7%. That air-yards number is the interesting one, because his average depth of target was only 11.8 yards, WR99. He's not a pure deep threat, he's just the first read on everything that travels. Kellen Moore and Doug Nussmeier are back running the same offense that took his target share from 18.8% to 29.4% in one year. There's no new-system risk here.

The honest worry is the games column. Our 15-game expectation comes with a range of 9 to 17, and the record explains why: 2024 ended after week 9 with a concussion, 2025 ended after week 17 with an illness. The low tail in our full range is from seasons cut short like that. He still cleared 15 points in 8 of 16 weeks last year and beat the position's weekly median all 16 times. Take him at 18, don't reach into the teens, and let him fall if the room sleeps.

name: De'Von Achane
body_compact: He hit the position's weekly median in all 16 games last year, and that's the whole pitch. Twenty points a game, RB5, target share climbing to 19.4%, one spot behind Bijan. The downside is real: our projection has him at 14 games with a range down to 9, and the sheet already carries an IR designation from October. There's also a 17.1-point cliff behind his tier, so the top of this group holds up. Draft him at his ADP of 21.2 if the games number doesn't scare you, and he's worth a round earlier if it doesn't.
body_full:
Sixteen for sixteen. That's the fact that decides Achane's case: he beat the position's weekly median in every game he played last season, 20.1 points a game on his way to RB5 among 147 qualifying backs. He cleared 15 points in 14 of those 16 weeks and his worst was 12.8. When he plays, he returns draft capital every single week, which almost nobody at this ADP can claim.

The role keeps widening. His target share jumped from 15.3% in 2024 to 19.4% in 2025, third among running backs and one spot behind Bijan Robinson, with 481 receiving yards that ranked RB5. The passing game is where his edge lives, and the books posted his receptions line at 4.5 for a reason. The one thing he doesn't give you is goal-line work: 13.3% red-zone share of his own touches ranked RB89, and his 43 red-zone touches were only RB16. He scores through space, not through the pile.

So the downside is games, and the sheet says so plainly: our number assumes 14, with a realistic range of 9 to 17, and it already lists him on IR as of October 11. The low tail of his outcomes comes from seasons cut short by injury, and 2023's 11-game year shows what that looks like. He's also playing for a new play caller in Bobby Slowik under a first-year head coach, which cuts both ways. Our number puts him at 245 points, RB3 on our board, about 20 points above what backs drafted at his ADP have historically returned. I'd take him a round earlier than his 21.2 ADP and accept the injury risk, because the weekly hit rate pays for the missed weeks.

name: CeeDee Lamb
body_compact: Our number puts him at 291 points, WR5, and that is 34.6 points better than the pool of receivers drafted around pick 9. The case rests on a 25% target share worth 10.1 a game, but last season was real: 200.9 points over 13 games, WR21, with a low 14.4% red-zone share of his own touches. The 2025 season is the whole argument against him, so start there. 200.9 points over 13 games, WR21 among 228 receivers, 15.4 a game, 76 total touches at WR18. Even in that down year he cleared the position's weekly median in 12 of 13 weeks and finished WR10 in receiving yards, which tells you the usage never left, only the touchdowns did. The red-zone profile is the real crack: just 14.4% of his touches inside the red zone, WR73, with only 17 red-zone touches. That is where 2023's 401.2-point, WR1 season came from, and it is the gap between WR5 and WR21.

The books posted his receiving line at 76.5 yards and 6.5 catches, and Dallas ran 56% situation-neutral passes at 30.6 seconds a play, so the offense itself should keep feeding him. A 25% target share worth 10.1 a game and 73.1% snap share carry that projection, and he sits at the top of a tier with one player left before a 17.4-point cliff. George Pickens is listed second in Dallas, so the target pie has a real second slice now, and that is the fact to watch.

The shoulder ended his 2024 after week 16 and he missed weeks 4 to 6 last year, so 10 to 17 games is the honest range around the 15 expected. Pick 9 is fair if the touchdowns come back. I'd draft him there and count myself lucky if a down year in the record scares anyone off.

name: Jahmyr Gibbs
body_compact: Two straight years of RB1-level scoring, 362.9 in 2024 and 366.6 in 2025, and last season he beat the position's weekly median in 16 of 17 games. Our number has him at 262, RB1 on our board, and he's going around pick 3, which is fine when the historical return at that slot is about 242 and he clears it by 20. The real cost is the red zone, RB36 in share of his own touches, plus a games range that runs 9 to 17. Draft him at 1.1 and stop overthinking it.
body_full:
Sixteen of seventeen weeks above the position's median last season. That's the whole case in one line, and it's why our number puts him at 262 points, RB1 on our board, even though our projection sits well under the 366.6 he actually scored in 2025. The gap is mostly games math. We expect 15 of them, with a realistic range of 9 to 17, and two straight 17-game seasons tell you the healthy version shows up most of the time.

The role is still stretching. His target share climbed from 12.1% in 2024 to 17.1% last year, third among 147 qualifying backs in receiving yards and one spot behind Bijan Robinson in both yards and overall scoring. Campbell and Morton are both back, so the setup doesn't change. One thing does hold him back, and it's the scoring distribution. His red-zone share of his own touches was just 19.9%, RB36 among 146, even though his 67 red-zone touches ranked third at the position. He gets into the scoring area plenty but splits the shortest finishes, and that's where his ceiling gets trimmed next to backs who own their goal line outright.

Drafters are taking him around pick 3, and the books have posted him at 83.5 rush yards, 4.5 receptions and 30.5 receiving yards a game, which reads like a back who wins through the air as much as on the ground. History says backs drafted there return about 242 points with busts pooled in, and our number sits 20 above that. That's a projection backed by production, not a leap. If you're picking at the top of 1.1, take him and move on. If Bijan is on the board instead, that's the only argument worth having.

name: Amon-Ra St. Brown
body_compact: Three straight seasons at WR3, never missing a game the last two years, and Detroit kept the whole offense intact. The 31% target share grew from 27% the year before, and 36 red-zone touches led all receivers. Three straight years at WR3 and not a single game missed in either of the last two seasons. That's the whole case in one breath, and it's why our number puts him at 295 points, WR4 at the position, while drafters take him around pick 5. That ADP feels about right against a historical average near 258 for receivers drafted there. We project him 36.7 points above that, mostly because the usage keeps climbing. His target share went from 27.0% in 2024 to 31.3% last season, fourth among all receivers, and it's worth over 10 points a game on its own.

The role is short and steady. An 8.1-yard average depth of target ranks near the very bottom of the league, so he isn't winning you weeks on chunk plays. He's winning them on volume and finishing: 36 red-zone touches led the position, 21 inside the ten trailed only Davante Adams, and he beat the weekly median in 16 of 17 games. Week 15's 41.4 was the spike, but the base rate is the story.

The one crack in the wall: only 20.6% of his own touches come in the red zone, WR32 among qualifying receivers, so the touchdown upside leans on Detroit getting him the ball down there rather than on his own usage near the goal line. That's worth watching but not worth passing on. Campbell and Morton both return, he's listed first among Detroit's receivers, and the books posted his receiving line at 77.5 yards and 6.5 catches. Draft him at his ADP and move on.

name: Jaxon Smith-Njigba
body_compact: He led all receivers in receiving yards last season and finished WR2 overall, one spot behind Puka Nacua, so this is not a projection bet anymore, it is a payoff for what he already did. name: Ja'Marr Chase
body_compact: A 32% target share on a team passing 63% of the time is the whole case, and it is worth over ten points a game by our number. The catch is the year-over-year slide: 23.71 points a game in 2024, 19.6 last year, and his red-zone share sits at WR106, so the touchdowns have to come from volume. The usage is as heavy as it gets: a 32.3% target share and a 94.4% snap share, both top-three at the position, on an offense Zac Taylor calls himself and passes 63% of the time. name: Puka Nacua
body_compact: He's my WR1 and he finished last season as the actual WR1, 375 points in 16 games while clearing the position's weekly median 15 of 16 times. The engine behind it is a 30% target share worth over 10 points a game by our numbers. The target share is the whole case. 30% of the Rams' targets, worth +10.1 a game in our model even after netting out seven factors, and he turns it into points because McVay still calls the plays and feeds him 139 touches, best at the position last year. Worth noting his red-zone share of touches was just 10.2%, so a chunk of his scoring runs through yardage, but he scored over the position's weekly median in 15 of 16 weeks anyway, with a 46.5-bomb in week 16. The ADP has actually slipped, from 2.8 to 4.2 over ten days in September, and I don't get it. Two players remain in his tier before a 23.4-point cliff. I'd grab him at 3.3 and feel great about it.

name: Justin Jefferson

The usage never left. He ran routes on 94% of the snaps and pulled in a 30% target share last season, both top-7 among all qualifying receivers, on a team O'Connell still calls plays for. And that's the real downside you have to weigh. He went from 18.68 points a game in 2024 to 11.85 in 2025, finished WR19, and cleared 15 points only four times in 17 weeks. His best week was 22.6. name: LaJohntay Wester
body_compact: He played one snap-count game all of 2025 and scored -2 points in it, dead last among qualifying receivers, and he opens this year sixth on a Baltimore depth chart behind Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman. But sixth on the depth chart behind Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Ja'Kobi Lane and Devontez Walker is not a rotation spot, and our expected 13 games with a 6-to-17 range only counts if he is active to use them. There is no ADP on file and just two players in his tier before a steep drop, which tells you drafters agree. My call: let him go in every draft. If he lands on your radar in year three with a real role, that is the time to care.

The games question is real too. Two straight seasons of 12 games, and the realistic range this year runs 8 to 17. He is 29.5 and entering year eight. O'Connell still runs the offense and calls the plays himself, so nothing is changing about the role, and Hockenson sits ahead of him on the depth chart as of early September.

Our number puts him at 57 points, TE59 on our board, and drafters take him around pick 361. That is late enough that he costs you nothing, but the pick does more good on a bench RB with actual upside. Let him go unless you are a Minnesota believer carrying three tight ends and a deep bench.

name: Jackson Hawes
body_compact: Third on the depth chart behind Kincaid and Knox, and the target share showed it last year at 5.3%, TE90 among qualifying tight ends. His touchdown share costs him 0.7 points a game. Four points a week in 2025, never a 15-point week. Both the head coach and the play caller are new this year, so there is no track record of them using him at all. He got just 3 red-zone touches all last season, TE61 among qualifying tight ends. Let him go at pick 368 and stream elsewhere.
body_full:
Buffalo listed him third among their tight ends behind Dalton Kincaid and Dawson Knox, and the 2025 usage matched the label. A 5.3% target share, TE90 among 126 qualifying tight ends, with 16 touches all season. He averaged 4.0 points a game and his best week was 9.6, so the weekly median beat him more often than not. He was on the field for 13 of 17 games and never missed one to injury, so the other four were healthy scratches. His snap share sat at 40% to 41% whether you look at the first month or the last four weeks, so the role never grew as the season went on.

The scoring role is the real drag. His touchdown share comes in at 1.1x and costs him 0.7 points a game, on just 3 red-zone touches and 2 inside the ten last year. Short average depth of target at 7.3 yards does not help him chase chunk points either. A new play caller in Pete Carmichael Jr. could shuffle the tight end pecking order, but nothing on file says it shuffles toward him.

Our number has him at 58 points, TE56 on our board, and drafters take him around pick 368, so nobody is reaching for him. That is the right instinct. If you are rostering a third tight end this late, take a flier on a role you can actually see rather than a block-first backup. Let him go and check back if the depth chart changes.

name: Jonnu Smith
body_compact: A 31-year-old second tight end behind Tucker Kraft in LaFleur's offense, and the numbers tell you what that means: 5.0 points a game in 2025, target share cut from 19.5% to 10.4%. His average depth of target was 4.3 yards, TE83 among 125 qualifying tight ends, and he cleared 15 points in zero of his 17 weeks. He played all 17 weeks, so this isn't an availability story, it's a role story. Our number has him at 62 points, TE53. Let him go entirely unless your league rosters three tight ends.
body_full:
The fall is the whole note. Two seasons ago Jonnu Smith averaged 13.08 a game and finished TE4. Last year he averaged 5.01, his target share dropped from 19.5% to 10.4%, and he never once cleared 15 points in 17 weeks. He didn't miss a game to get there, either, so you can't wave it off as bad luck. The role shrank.

The move to Green Bay doesn't fix that on its own. He's listed second among GB tight ends behind Tucker Kraft, and Kraft isn't going anywhere. LaFleur calls the plays himself and the GB offense ran 51% situation-neutral passes last year, which sounds nice until you notice Smith's snap share slid from 58% early in 2025 to 38% late. The touch profile got shallow too: his average depth of target was 4.3 yards, TE83 among 125 qualifying tight ends. He saw 9 red-zone touches, TE25 among 126, but only 3 inside the ten, so the scoring chances were thin even where he did get fed. Thirty-one years old, tenth season, and the offense he's joining already has a tight end it trusts.

Our number puts him at 62 points, TE53 on our board, with most outcomes between 46 and 78. Drafters take him around pick 328, which is rounds after our number says he's worth a roster spot anyway. If you're drafting him at all it's as a third tight end in the deepest format in your league, and the bye-week plug at week 11 is about the ceiling of the job. I'd rather use the pick on a receiver with a path to actual targets.

name: Nate Boerkircher
body_compact: A second-round rookie stuck behind Brenton Strange, and the depth chart from September 4 has him second among JAX tight ends. Our number has him at 64 points, TE49, which is not a draftable stat line in most leagues. The real risk is the expected 13 games, with a range of 6 to 17 once injury enters it. He is going around pick 377, so he costs nothing, but I would rather spend that pick on a running back lottery ticket than wait on a rookie who cannot see the field yet.
body_full:
He went 56th overall in the draft, so the Jaguars spent real draft capital on him, and then they lined him up behind Brenton Strange on the depth chart to start the season. That combination is the whole case. A round 2 tight end with a second-string label in September is a stash, not a contributor, and our board backs that up: TE49, 64 projected points, with most outcomes landing between 46 and 83.

The reason to care anyway is the profile. Strange is not a locked-in star, the Jags won 13 games last year and passed on 59% of their situation-neutral plays, so there are targets floating around this offense. If the rookie climbs the depth chart at any point, the second-round investment means they'll want him involved. The problem is you cannot project that climb from anything on this sheet. No headlines, no injury designation, no usage to point at. He's a blank slate, and blank slates at tight end in redraft leagues are usually just empty roster spots.

He's going around pick 377, which is a final-round flier in most leagues, and our number has him at 253 overall, so the gap is real but modest. The expected 13 games with a range of 6 to 17 tells you the season could go sideways fast. If you have a third tight end spot and want to hold the guy with draft capital, fine, take him with your last pick and let week 7's bye pass without stress. But if your bench is tight, a veteran TE2 who actually catches passes beats a lottery ticket. I'd only roster him if I could cut him in October without a second thought.

name: Rashod Bateman
body_compact: He averaged 4.1 points a game last season, and his target share fell from 15.8% to 11.4%. The crowded room costs him about 0.9 a game. He sat second on the depth chart behind Zay Flowers as of September 4, and in 2025 he cleared 15 points in just 1 of 13 weeks. Two years ago he put up 174.6 points and finished WR40, so the talent showed up before last year did not. Our number is 122 points, and drafters take him around pick 227, later than his record deserves. He is a last-round flier, nothing more, and only if you need Baltimore exposure.
body_full:
A 15.8% target share in 2024 became 11.4% in 2025, and his scoring followed it down from 10.91 points a game to 4.11. That is the whole case in one line. He was WR102 in 2025 with one week over 15 points and a zero in week 5. He is 26.8, a former first-rounder, and listed second behind Zay Flowers, so the talent draft pick still carries some weight. But a new head coach in Jesse Minter and a new play caller in Declan Doyle mean no one owes him anything.

The crowded room costs him about 0.9 points a game, and there is real competition behind him in Ja'Kobi Lane and Devontez Walker. The one thing on his side is the team: the books posted 11.5 wins on Baltimore, so the offense should score. Red-zone usage was actually decent, WR29 in his own touches, and 8 red-zone touches despite the collapse.

Our number is 122 points, WR62, with the middle range 97 to 147. Drafters take him around pick 227, well after that, and past receivers in that spot scored about 112.6. So he is going later than he should, and our number still likes him a little. I would take him in the last rounds as a bench flier, but I would not count on him for anything before week 13's bye. If he shows anything early, he is a free add. If he opens like 2025, let him go.

name: Chig Okonkwo
body_compact: Our number has him at 94 points, about 16 clear of what TEs drafted around his ADP have actually produced, and he sits first on the WSH depth chart. But the usage screams checkdown: a 6.3% red-zone share of his own touches, TE97 in that group, and an average target 4.6 yards downfield. He cleared 15 points once all last season. The change from TEN to WAS is why we still like him, since that offense should give him more catches to harvest. He is going around pick 177 and I would take him a round earlier as my TE2.
body_full:
The move from TEN to WAS is the whole reason to draft him, and the reason he is our TE22 with 94 points, about 16 more than TEs drafted around his ADP have historically delivered. Washington threw on 50% of situation-neutral plays and ran 33.6 seconds a play in 2025, a faster, more pass-happy setup than anything he had in Tennessee, and he is listed first among their tight ends with only John Bates and Ben Sinnott behind him. That is a real path to a steady catch count.

The downside is what the usage actually is. His target share was 14.9% last year, and of his own touches only 6.3% came in the red zone, TE97 among 126 qualifying tight ends. His average target traveled 4.6 yards, TE73 in that group. So he eats targets near the line of scrimmage and almost never scores, which is why he cleared 15 points once in 17 weeks and bottomed out at 0. He has beaten the position's weekly median in 12 of 17 games, so he pads a lineup without ever winning you one. His season-by-season line backs that up: 124, 111.6 and 113.4 points the last three years, always a TE20-ish finish, never a spike.

Availability is not a question. He has missed just one game in three seasons, and there is no injury designation on file right now. Drafters are taking him around pick 177, and he has drifted down the board this week. I would grab him a round earlier than that as a second tight end. You are paying for a reliable 7-point week, not a spike, and the new offensive play caller in Washington is the swing factor that could push him past that.

name: Makai Lemon
body_compact: A first-round rookie (pick 20) listed third on the PHI depth chart behind DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks, in an offense that ran 54% situation-neutral passes. Our number has him at 136 points, a touch above the usual outcome for WRs taken around pick 108. The real downside is availability: he is expected to play 15 games, but the realistic range runs from 9 to 17 if injuries hit. He is worth a pick around 108, and I would even go a round earlier than his ADP given the offense around him.
body_full:
The reason to draft Makai Lemon is the situation he walked into, not anything he has put on tape yet. Philadelphia threw on 54% of situation-neutral plays last year, won 11 games, and Vegas has posted a 10.5 win total for them this season. A first-round pick at pick 20 landing in an offense that good and that pass-heavy is the whole case. Our number puts him at 136 points, and he goes around pick 108, so he is roughly a round later than he should be.

The honest snag is the depth chart, checked September 4th. He is listed third among PHI wideouts, behind DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks, with Marquise Brown and Elijah Moore below him. Third on the list in week one is not a death sentence for a rookie, but it means the points have to come to him rather than being handed over. Watch the snap counts in the first month before you decide if he has cleared Wicks.

The downside that matters is games played. We project 15, with a realistic range of 9 to 17 once injury risk is in, and seasons that bottom out at 86 points are the ones cut short. That is the swing you accept. My call: take him at his ADP of about 108, or a few picks earlier if you believe a rookie third receiver in this offense becomes a starter by midseason. He is a roster-shaping pick, not a safe one.

name: Jacory Croskey-Merritt
body_compact: The new play caller is the whole question here. Last year he was RB33 on 184 touches with a 38.5% snap share, and only 7 of 17 weeks beat the position median, so the role was thin even while he stayed healthy all 17 games. The scoring profile drags too: that touchdown-points share costs him about 6.2 a game, and a 3.0% target share means no receiving cushion. Still, he sits first on the depth chart and our number has him about 9 points over his ADP peers. I'd take him a round after pick 114, not before.
body_full:
Dan Quinn stays, but David Blough is new as the play caller, and that's the one thing that could swing a second-year seventh-round pick who finished last year as RB33 off 184 touches. The depth chart lists him first, with Rachaad White and Kaytron Allen behind, but the usage never got fat in 2025: 38.5% snap share, a 3.0% target share, 17% of his own touches in the red zone. Seven of seventeen weeks above the position median, one 27-point week, and a worst of 1.7. That's a touchdown-or-nothing shape.

The scoring profile is the real drag. His 34.2% touchdown-points share costs him about 6.2 points a game, and only 10.6% of his touches came inside the ten, worth another 1.4. Sixty-eight receiving yards all season means he can't fall back on passing game work when the touchdowns don't come. He did see 20 touches inside the ten last year, RB21 among 147 qualifying backs, so the chances were there.

Our number has him at 105, about 9 points over backs drafted near pick 114, with most outcomes between 83 and 128. We expect him for 15 games, with a realistic range of 9 to 17 once injury risk is in. The books posted his rush yard line at 40.5, which tells you they expect a modest workload too. There's also a Q designation as of September 9, so check that before you click. Seven players sit in his tier before a 10.1-point drop. I'd let him fall past pick 114 and take him a few picks later, with White as the fallback if the new caller shifts the backfield.

name: Rachaad White
body_compact: He's a backup now, listed second behind Jacory Croskey-Merritt in Washington, and the year he just had doesn't argue for a rescue: 8.4 points a game, above the position median in only 10 of 17, down from 13.31 the year before. Our number has him at 119 points, RB36, while drafters still take him around pick 113. That's a round earlier than he should go for a guy whose pass-game role shrank too, target share down to 8.3%. body_full:
The decline is real, not a one-week blip. He went from 13.31 points a game in 2024 to 8.41 last year, his target share fell from 10.8% to 8.3%, and the pass-catching piece was always what made him playable. The role is the problem on top of that. He was already splitting time at 50.6% of snaps last season, and now he's listed second in Washington behind Jacory Croskey-Merritt as of week one. A 27-year-old backup running back on a 7.5-win team doesn't get to a fantasy starting number without injuries ahead of him, and you can't draft around pick 113 counting on that.

Drafters are moving the right direction and still not far enough. His ADP slid 10.6 picks in four days, from 119 to 129.6, and I'd let it keep sliding. Our number has him at 119 points, RB36, and he sits in a tier of 11 guys before a 10.1-point cliff, so there's no urgency to grab him before the drop. He also carries a Q designation into week 1, which is one more reason not to spend a real pick here. If he somehow wins the job outright or Croskey-Merritt gets hurt, you can add him off the wire. In drafts, let him go.

name: Kyle Monangai
body_compact: A seventh-round rookie who played all 17 games and still only saw 41.4% of the snaps, now sitting second on the depth chart behind D'Andre Swift. The fantasy case is goal-line work: 39 red-zone touches, RB22 at the position, while the passing game gives him nothing, 164 receiving yards and an average depth of target of 0.1 yards. He is also flagged Q as of September 9. Our number has him at 119 points, about 15 better than the historical outcome at his ADP, so he is worth a pick around 118. I would take him a round later than that and be happy.
body_full: The reason to draft Monangai is the goal-line work, not the volume. Last season he got 39 red-zone touches and 20 inside the ten, both top-22 among 147 qualifying backs, on a Ben Johnson offense that won 11 games. That role is what keeps him fantasy-relevant even while he took only 41.4% of the snaps and sits second behind D'Andre Swift on the September depth chart. Johnson calls the plays himself and is back, so if the touchdowns keep coming, the path is intact. The passing game is where he loses you weeks: 164 receiving yards all of last year, an average depth of target of 0.1 yards, and a 5.6% target share. Still, he handled 187 touches, RB28 among 147 qualifying backs, so the workload behind that role was real, not a trick of a few big games. His best week hit 22.8 in week 9, and he beat the position's weekly median in 9 of his 17 games, so when the touchdowns land the good weeks are genuine spike weeks. The games question matters too. He is flagged Q as of September 9, and the expectation is 14 games with a realistic range of 8 to 17. Our number of 119 points already accounts for some missed time, and it sits about 15 points above what running backs drafted around pick 118 have historically delivered. There are 12 players in his tier before a 10.1-point cliff, so you are not losing much by waiting. My call: take him a few picks after his ADP in the double-digit rounds, but draft a back with passing-game work first, because the week-to-week scoring here is lumpy.

name: TreVeyon Henderson
body_compact: He's already ruled out for the opener, and that's the whole draft in miniature: the talent showed up last year, the role might not. He averaged 12.1 points a game as a rookie, second on the depth chart behind Rhamondre Stevenson, and our number has him at 120 points, RB34, basically even with what running backs drafted around pick 72 have delivered. A 29.1% touchdown-points share costs him 2.9 a game when the scores dry up. I'm waiting a few picks after his ADP. Let him fall to me there, and I'll grab him. Earlier is a reach.
body_full:
He's ruled out for week 1 already, and that frames everything about drafting him this summer. He played all 17 games as a rookie, so the availability question is new, and our number expects 13 of them this year with a realistic range of 7 to 17. That's the swing you're signing up for.

The role is the real hesitation. He was second among NE backs on the September depth chart behind Rhamondre Stevenson, played 45.8% of snaps last year, and got 18% of his own touches in the red zone. Our projection puts those usage factors together at roughly 7.5 points a game working against him, led by a 29.1% touchdown-points share worth -2.9 a game. When the touchdowns stop coming at last year's rate, there isn't much underneath. He cleared 15 points in only 4 of 17 weeks, and his worst was 0.5.

The good news: 12.1 points a game as a rookie, 24 touches inside the ten, RB13 in that scoring-range count, and the same coaching staff in Vrabel and McDaniels. Our number is 120 points, RB34, right in line with what backs drafted around pick 72 have produced, about 119. So the draft spot is fair, not a steal. There are 13 players in his tier before a 10.1-point cliff, so I'm not rushing. Let him come to me a few picks after his ADP and take him as a bench back with a real top-of-lineup week in him, like that 32.3 in week 11.

name: Dalton Kincaid
body_compact: Kincaid's per-game jump to 10.5 points last year is the reason to draft him, and the 571 receiving yards back it up. The catch: his target share fell from 20.2% to 14.6%, and the snap share sat at 37.6%, TE71, so the role is thin even if the efficiency was real. Our number has him at 118, a hair above what TEs drafted around pick 112 usually give you, and that assumes 13 games from a guy who has missed time two years running. He's fine at his ADP as your second tight end, but I'm not reaching a round earlier.
body_full:
The efficiency is real and it's the whole case. He beat the position's weekly median in 10 of 12 games last year, he averaged 10.5 a game, and his 571 yards were TE16 despite playing only 12 weeks. When Kincaid is on the field, he produces. The problem is what's on the field around him: a 37.6% snap share, TE71 among qualifying tight ends, and a target share that dropped from 20.2% to 14.6%. That's not a guy being force-fed, that's a guy cashing the few looks he gets at an average depth of 9.5 yards, TE8. New play caller Pete Carmichael Jr. is the swing factor drafters can't figure out yet, and it's part of why he's going a round later than he should.

Then the games. He played 12 in 2025 and 13 in 2024, both with missed weeks plus healthy weeks he didn't suit up for. Our 13-game expectation has a realistic range of 7 to 17. That variance is why our number sits at 118, only about 4 points above what tight ends drafted around pick 112 have actually delivered once the busts are pooled in. He's not offering points over replacement, he's offering a clean week-to-week producer if the 12-game version shows up 15 times.

The call: at ADP 112, he's fine. I wouldn't take him a round earlier and I wouldn't let him slip past 130. Draft him as your second tight end and hope the new offense widens that snap share, because the talent showed up last year even when the volume didn't.

name: Jaxson Dart
body_compact: The rushing volume is the whole case: 41 touches a season ago, QB3 among 64 qualifiers, one spot behind Josh Allen, with 18 red-zone touches and 10 inside the ten. That usage on a bad 4-win offense still got him 240 points, QB13. Our number has him at 252 and QB12, basically even with what quarterbacks drafted around pick 99 have done. The real downside is availability, 14 expected games but a range of 8 to 17, and he already missed two weeks as a rookie. At ADP 98.5 I'd take him, maybe a round earlier.
body_full:
Dart ran his way into the QB conversation as a rookie and the volume is why. 41 total touches, QB3 among 64 qualifiers, one spot behind Josh Allen, plus 18 red-zone touches and 10 inside the ten, also QB3. That's scoring-range usage you usually only see from the elite runner-quarterbacks, and it produced 240 points and a QB13 finish in 14 games on a team that won 4 games. He cleared 15 points in 10 of his 14 played weeks, and his best was a 28.42-point week 7. If the Giants are merely competent this year, that per-week number climbs.

Our number has him at 252, QB12 on our board, which is basically dead even with what quarterbacks drafted around pick 99 have historically delivered. So at ADP 98.5 you're not paying for hope, you're paying for the median outcome. The books posted his rush yards at just 29.5, which feels light given how much he ran last year. Their win total on the Giants sits at 7.5, and he gets CLE at home in week 15 and DAL in week 17 if you're thinking playoff pushes.

The real risk is games played. He missed weeks 11 and 12 as a rookie, our model expects 14 starts with a realistic range of 8 to 17, and the style that gets him those touches also gets him hit. New staff too, John Harbaugh running the show with Matt Nagy calling plays, and Jameis Winston behind him if anything goes sideways. I'd still take him at pick 99, even a round earlier in a superflex league, because the rushing usage makes his good weeks top-five weeks.

name: Kyle Pitts Sr.
body_compact: Pitts Sr. broke out last season and drafters haven't caught up. He was TE2, one spot behind Trey McBride in points, touches and yards, and his target share jumped from 13.7% to 22.8%. The catch: only 10.2% of his touches came in the red zone, TE88 among 126, so the big weeks came from volume and chunk plays, not scoring. A brand-new staff in Atlanta with Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees adds unknowns. He played all 17 games three straight years, so the durability worry is thin. He's our TE5 but going around pick 78, a round later than he should. Draft him.
body_full:
Pitts finished last season TE2 and drafters are taking him around pick 78, late round 7. That gap is the whole case. He scored 211 points, sat one spot behind Trey McBride in points, touches and yards, and beat the position's weekly median in 14 of 17 games. He's our TE5 at rank 109, and the TEs drafted where he's going historically put up about 130 points. Our number has him at 150, twenty points clear of that. You're getting a top-five tight end a round or so later than he should go, in the stretch where managers grab their QB2.

The thing to understand is how he scored. His red-zone share of touches was 10.2%, TE88 among 126 qualifying tight ends, and he cleared 15 points in only 4 of 17 weeks. The points came from a 22.8% target share and 928 yards, not from touchdowns. That makes the new regime matter more for him than for almost anyone. Kevin Stefanski is a new head coach and Tommy Rees a new play caller. If they keep feeding him 88 touches, the TE2 repeat is live. If they reshape the offense, the path narrows.

The durability angle is clean. Three straight seasons of 17 of 17 games, no reserve-list stints, and he's 25.9 entering year six. The books posted him at 41.5 receiving yards and 4.5 receptions, modest lines for a guy who averaged 12.4 a game. I'd take him a round earlier than his ADP rather than wait, and if he's still sitting there a few picks after pick 78 in your room, that's a steal.

name: Dak Prescott
body_compact: He played all 17 last year and finished QB6 at 18.2 points a game, two seasons after a hamstring cost him weeks 10 through 18 in 2024. That availability swing is the whole draft debate: we expect 14 games, with a real range of 8 to 17. Our number has him at 274 points, QB5, basically dead even with what quarterbacks drafted around pick 78 have scored historically. The playcalling stays intact under Klayton Adams and he sits alone atop the depth chart. Draft him at 77.5 and you are getting a top-five arm at QB7 money, just know a missed month is the risk you signed up for.
body_full:
The hamstring that ended his 2024 after week 9 is the one thing I keep coming back to, because it is the difference between the QB3 he was in 2023 and the QB31 he was a year later. Last season he answered it: 17 of 17, 309 points, QB6, and he beat the weekly median in 12 of those 17 starts. Our number has him at 274 with a middle range of 221 to 328, and the low end of the full tails comes from seasons cut short by injury, which is exactly the history here.

We expect 14 games, and that is where the draft call lives. Quarterbacks taken around pick 78 have averaged about 273.7 points with busts and injuries pooled in, and our number sits 0.6 points from that, so the draft is paying him like the availability risk he is rather than the QB5 our board says. If he gives you 17 again, the 328 end of the range is live and he beats every passer drafted in that stretch.

Nothing about the situation argues against it. Same head coach in Brian Schottenheimer, Klayton Adams still calling plays, and no other quarterback even listed on the September depth chart release. The 2024 to 2025 jump in points per game, 14.57 to 18.18, held over a full season, so I read it as real. My call: take him right at 77.5, or a round earlier if you want certainty at the position, and accept that a lost month is the scenario that sinks the pick.

name: DJ Moore
body_compact: Three straight 17-game seasons, then a move from Chicago to Buffalo, and yet his numbers fell off a cliff: points per game dropped from 13.89 to 9.92 and target share from 26.6% to 16.0% in one year. He still ran routes on 84.8% of snaps, top-20 among receivers, so the workload habit is intact. The downside is a crowded depth chart with Shakir and Coleman eating looks, worth almost a full point a game against him. We have him at 207 points, ahead of where drafters take him around pick 52. I'd draft him there.
body_full:
He played all 17 games three seasons running, and that availability is the quiet engine of this case. We expect 14 games with a realistic span of 9 to 17, and even trimmed down he lands inside a middle range of 169 to 244 points. Our number puts him at 207, about 21 points better than what receivers drafted around pick 52 have historically produced, busts pooled in. So he is going a round or so later than he should.

Now the uncomfortable part. His points per game fell from 13.89 in 2024 to 9.92 in 2025, and his target share collapsed from 26.6% to 16.0%. That is not a small drift, that is a role change. He was still on the field for 84.8% of snaps, top-20 at the position, which tells you the staff never stopped trusting him. The touches just stopped coming, and the red-zone work dried up: 13 red-zone touches, a 13.0% share of his own touches, bottom half of the league. A touchdown load worth negative points a game caps how high this can go.

Buffalo is the swing. New head coach in Joe Brady, new play caller, a team the books posted at 10.5 wins, and a target room with Shakir and Coleman already in it. The depth chart lists him first, but that room is crowded and it costs him. My read: the 2025 usage dip is the risk you're drafting, and the Bills' passing volume is the reward. If the target share rebuilds even partway toward 2024, he beats this number comfortably. I'd draft him at his ADP and not a pick earlier, and I'd want to see week 1 targets before believing the bounce-back fully.

name: Matthew Caldwell
body_compact: He's already on IR as of September 9, and we project him for 3 points with 0 games expected, maybe 1 if things break right. He's a 23-year-old undrafted rookie sitting fourth on the Rams' QB list behind Stafford and Ty Simpson, and McVay runs an offense that doesn't need a fourth arm on the field. Vegas posted an 11.5 win total for this team, a number that says they're trying to win now with zero patience for a developmental arm. There's no ADP because there's no reason to draft him. Leave him off the board entirely.
body_full:
The IR designation landed on September 9, before the season even really started, and that's the whole case. We have him at 0 games played, with 1 as the ceiling once injury risk is in the math, and our season number is 3 points with a middle range of -2 to 8.
